extracted.intended_audience: university instructors, instructional designers, online course developers, and distance-education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, selecting, and theorizing about online learning modes, interactions, technologies, and PLAR (prior learning assessment and recognition) practices in higher education and distance-learning contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of interaction (student–teacher; student–student; student–content)
rubrics_metrics.description: The three primary forms of interaction in online learning are student–teacher, student–student, and student–content; sufficient levels of deep and meaningful learning can be developed as long as one of these three forms of interaction is at very high levels. The other two may be offered at minimal levels or even eliminated without degrading the educational experience. (Anderson 2003b)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the relative emphasis among these interactions based on costs, content, learning objectives, convenience, technology, and time availability. Teachers and designers should plan an appropriate mix of student, teacher, and content interaction uniquely designed for each learning outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-of-inquiry (collaborative) model characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The collaborative/community-of-inquiry model uses synchronous and asynchronous interactions (video, audio, computer conferencing, chats, or virtual world) to support social skills, collaboration, and the development of personal relationships among participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These environments are particularly rich but bind learners in time (group-paced) and are generally more expensive and less scalable; use when social interaction, group work, and relationship-building are central to learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent study model characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent learning relies on structured learning tools such as computer-assisted tutorials, drills, simulations, virtual labs, and texts; learners may be sequenced, directed, and credentialed by teachers but can interact directly with content they find on the Web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model scales better and can be supported by colleagues, peers, workplace mentors, and social software; appropriate where self-paced, individualized mastery of content or practice is the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose activities based on the nature of the prescribed learning
rubrics_metrics.description: A key deciding factor for teachers and designers is the nature of the learning that is prescribed: different learning outcomes are best learned through particular learning activities (Prensky's guiding question: not how students learn, but how do they learn what?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map intended outcomes to activity types (see Prensky mappings). Use the model of interactions to ensure an appropriate mix of student, teacher, and content interaction for each learning outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviours: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviours are learned through imitation, feedback, and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that provide models for imitation, frequent feedback loops, and opportunities for repeated practice (can be supported by drills, simulations, coaching).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity is learned through playing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate play-based, exploratory, or game-like activities to foster creative thinking; game forms and styles can be used online or offline to facilitate creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts are learned through association, drill, memory, and questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spaced repetition, drills, quizzes, and associative learning tasks to support factual recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment is learned through reviewing cases, asking questions, making choices, receiving feedback, and coaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide case reviews, decision-making scenarios, reflective questioning, and coaching feedback to develop judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is learned through imitation, practice, and immersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create opportunities for modeled language use, frequent practice, and immersive experiences (e.g., interaction with native speakers or authentic content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation is learned through viewing examples and feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exemplars, demonstrations, and guided observation tasks with feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures are learned through imitation and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stepwise modeling and repeated practice opportunities (simulations, guided tasks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes are learned through system analysis, deconstruction, and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that break complex processes into components, include analysis tasks, and provide practice integrating steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems are learned through discovering principles and graduated tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scaffold tasks to lead learners from principles discovery to progressively complex applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning is learned through puzzles, problems, and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use problem-based learning, puzzles, worked examples, and opportunities for reflection on reasoning strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skills (physical or mental): how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Skills are learned through imitation, feedback, continuous practice, and increasing challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide modeled performance, iterative practice with feedback, and gradually increase task difficulty (e.g., virtual labs, simulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speeches or performance roles: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches or performance roles are learned by memorization, practice, and coaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include rehearsal opportunities, recording for review, and coach feedback for performance improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theories: how to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories are learned through logic, explanation, and questioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster activities that emphasize conceptual explanation, logical argumentation, and Socratic questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Semantic Web technologies to annotate and make content machine-readable
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic Web technologies allow annotating information using formal taxonomies so autonomous agents and humans can determine semantic meaning (e.g., label a data field as 'author’s telephone number' rather than formatting metadata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, describe content formally so agents can sort, query, format, and infer from data; be aware of the practical challenges in formally describing all web data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social tagging and emergent folksonomies
rubrics_metrics.description: User tagging and tracking (folksonomies) add self-organizational capacity to the Net, enabling harvesting, filtering, repurposing, and transformation of content through social technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage collaborative annotation/rating systems (e.g., CiteULike) to generate collective assessments and searchable shared resources for learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ autonomous agents to support learning tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Autonomous agents can perform roles such as intelligent searching (student-alerts), scheduling meetings, reminding students of deadlines, negotiating collaboration, providing remedial tuition, record keeping, monitoring progress, and even marking student communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate agent tools where they enhance efficiency and learner support, and match agent functions to pedagogical needs (examples: Google Alerts, meeting wizards, calendar reminders, tutoring agents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support reuse and adaptation of content via educational modelling languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational modelling languages and Semantic Web affordances allow formal description of content, activities, and learning context, facilitating reuse, adaptation, and distribution of digitized learning materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal descriptions where possible to enable affordable, reusable e-learning experiences; consider EML and similar standards for packaging learning units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design learning environments to be learner-, content-, community-, and assessment-centred
rubrics_metrics.description: The challenge for teachers and course developers is to construct e-learning environments that are simultaneously learner-centred, content-centred, community-centred, and assessment-centred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single best medium; instead develop a repertoire of online learning activities adaptable to diverse contexts and learner needs, and refine through feedback, assessment, and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLAR definition (Prior Learning Assessment and Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: PLAR is the formal acknowledgement of skills, knowledge, and competencies gained through work experience, informal training, and life experience (UNESCO definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat PLAR as a knowledge-building process that honours mature learners' experiential learning and can provide viable alternative learning opportunities in ODL contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLAR method: challenge-for-credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenge-for-credit allows learners to target a specific course, work with the course professor in a contractual relationship, and meet pre-established challenge conditions to demonstrate competency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method requires tailoring prior learning to pre-determined course-like knowledge clusters; it honours prior learning but may constrain learners to existing curricular categories and may not build new knowledge on top of prior experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLAR method: portfolio assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolio assessment permits learners to demonstrate prior knowledge through careful selection, reflection, connection, and projection of learning artefacts, enabling cognitive engagement with past experiences and the generation of new knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portfolio approaches are guided by university-provided criteria and outcomes; they allow learners fuller expression of prior knowledge and facilitate reflexive learning of self and professional identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional support structures for PLAR
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective PLAR implementation benefits from a central institutional structure (e.g., a central office) to champion, direct, and manage the PLAR process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized policy and management (as at Athabasca University) can make PLAR coherent and integrated across the institution and increase its effectiveness and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model building and outcome measurement for theory development
rubrics_metrics.description: Model-building is a first step in theory creation; after illustrating key variables and relationships, researchers and practitioners should theorize and measure the direction and magnitude of each variable's effect on outcomes such as learning, cost, completion, and satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presented models to form hypotheses, design studies, and pursue improvements in professional practice; measurement should focus on relevant outcome variables (learning, cost, completion, satisfaction).
